title: Platform Sharing and Visibility Architect Certification - Practice Exam
description: 60-question timed practice exam mirroring the official blueprint domain weights. 120 minutes, pass with 58% or higher.

questions.question: A user can edit the Account Rating field on the record page even though the field was removed from their page layout. What is the most likely reason?
options: FLS still grants edit permission for Rating
questions.explanation: Page layout absence does not revoke the FLS edit permission; the user can still edit via other surfaces or the field being FLS-editable. The fix is to set the field read-only in FLS, not just remove it from a layout.

questions.question: Why is removing a field from a page layout alone insufficient to secure a sensitive standard field?
options: Layout changes apply to all users
The field can still appear in search, list views, and reports where FLS is not honored
Layouts do not control standard objects
questions.explanation: Page layouts only affect record pages; search, list views, and reports surface fields by FLS, so a field visible in FLS but absent from a layout is still exposed in those surfaces.

questions.question: Which statement about field-level security is TRUE?
options: A user who can read an object always sees every field
Hidden fields are still returned by user-mode Apex SOQL unless enforced
Read-only fields are invisible to the user
FLS only applies to custom fields
questions.explanation: User-mode Apex returns hidden fields unless the code applies Security Enforced or StripInaccessible; FLS is not automatic in all code paths. Reading an object does not grant field visibility, and FLS applies to standard fields too.

questions.question: When is Apex Managed Sharing the correct tool rather than a sharing rule?
options: When the access criteria are too complex or dynamic for a criteria-based sharing rule
When you need to grant object-level permissions
When you want to restrict access
questions.explanation: Managed Sharing is for complex/dynamic record grants the declarative sharing model cannot express. It grants record access, never object permissions, and cannot restrict.

questions.question: A developer must return Case records to a Lightning component but hide any fields the calling user cannot read. Which is the correct pattern?
options: Return the full records and let the UI hide fields
Run the query in a 'without sharing' class
questions.explanation: stripInaccessible removes unreadable fields per the running user's FLS before the data reaches the client. Returning full records leaks them, 'without sharing' ignores record sharing, and UI hiding is not security.

questions.question: A batch job must modify records owned by users across many divisions, regardless of ownership, using a queueable that runs as the system. Which class declaration is appropriate and why?
options: 'without sharing' (or default system mode) because the operation is platform-context and must ignore record ownership
A permission set with View All
questions.explanation: A platform-triggered queueable that must act across ownership boundaries runs in system mode, which ignores record-level sharing. 'with sharing' would restrict it, and permissions/runAs do not change system-mode processing.

questions.question: A developer writes a Lightning action that returns Account records with a Compensation field. Managers can see it, reps cannot. What is the minimal robust fix?
options: Remove the field from the page layout
Add WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to the query or strip inaccessible fields before returning
questions.explanation: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED / stripInaccessible make the code honor FLS for the calling user, so reps receive the field stripped. Layouts and OWD do not make Apex honor field visibility.

questions.question: Which combination best protects a PII field end to end?
options: Classify it, hide via FLS, encrypt with Shield, and audit changes with field history
Only set the org-wide default to Private
questions.explanation: Layered protection - classify, restrict (FLS), encrypt at rest (Shield), and audit (field history) - is the model for sensitive data. Any single declarative change leaves a gap.

questions.question: Which mechanism best tailors record-page fields and picklist values to different business processes for the same object?
questions.explanation: Record types + page layouts vary the record page and picklist values by process. Compact layouts only affect the highlight panel, and FLS/Sharing do not define processes.

questions.question: What does System.runAs(testUser) accomplish in a test?
options: It runs the code as testUser so you can assert that user's effective record and field access
It only works on the system user
questions.explanation: runAs changes the running user within the test so you can verify the security model from that user's perspective. It does not disable sharing, grant permissions, or require the system user.

questions.question: Why does WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED sometimes throw an exception for a query that runs fine without it?
options: The object has too many fields
A selected field or object is not readable by the running user, and the enforcement is all-or-nothing
The query contains a formula field
questions.explanation: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is strict: any inaccessible field in the SELECT list raises an error rather than returning partial data. This is expected, intended behavior, not a bug.

questions.question: Why is a permission set group preferable to assigning several individual permission sets to a large cohort of users?
options: It bundles multiple permission sets so users receive the combined permissions with one assignment, and it supports dynamic assignment
It can remove a permission that the profile grants to all users
It changes the users' profile automatically
It grants record access without any object permissions
questions.explanation: A permission set group packages several permission sets for a single assignment and supports dynamic assignment rules, reducing admin overhead for large cohorts. It cannot remove profile permissions, change profiles, or grant record access by itself.

questions.question: Which statement about profiles versus permission sets is TRUE?
options: Permission sets can remove object permissions granted by the profile
A user must be assigned at least one permission set
Permission sets add permissions on top of the profile and never take them away
Profiles can be assigned multiple per user
questions.explanation: Permission sets are purely additive; the profile is the single baseline and permission sets extend it. A user can have zero permission sets and exactly one profile.

questions.question: Which statement about Apex sharing and field-level security is TRUE?
options: A 'without sharing' class automatically enforces field-level security
Apex in user mode must explicitly check field accessibility because SOQL does not enforce FLS by default
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED returns hidden fields but marks them read-only
Field accessibility cannot be checked in Apex
questions.explanation: Plain SOQL does not filter hidden fields; the developer must add WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED or Schema accessibility checks. System mode does not auto-enforce FLS, and WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED errors rather than silently returning hidden fields.

questions.question: Only HR managers should ever see records flagged with the custom field Sensitive__c = true; OWD is Public Read Only. Which declarative control delivers this?
options: A sharing rule granting HR managers access
A restriction rule on Sensitive__c = true granting only the HR managers group
questions.explanation: A restriction rule narrows the publicly visible set to only the HR managers group, blocking everyone else from the flagged records. A sharing rule would GRANT access and cannot remove it, and FLS/OWD do not filter by record criteria.

questions.question: Which is the recommended pattern for scaling a permission grant to a large, frequently-changing user population?
options: Edit the standard profile each time a new hire starts
Create a permission set group and use dynamic assignment rules on user attributes
Manually assign individual permission sets to each user
Set the object OWD to Public Read Only
questions.explanation: Dynamic assignment on a permission set group automatically covers joiners/leavers by filter criteria, the most scalable and least manual pattern.

questions.question: Which statement about cumulative sharing is TRUE?
options: Each access layer is mutually exclusive
A user's effective access is the UNION of OWD, hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, and relationship propagation - so map them together
questions.explanation: Effective access is the union of all layers; mapping the combination is essential because multiple layers can jointly expose a record even when each is individually correct.

questions.question: Which is the best way to keep managed-sharing volume and DML low?
options: Insert shares in a per-record trigger unconditionally
Compute the delta (new needed, existing unnecessary) and insert/delete in batches within one transaction
Use a different RowCause per record
questions.explanation: Reconciling the delta in batches minimizes both DML governors and sharing-table growth. Unconditional per-record inserts bloat sharing and can hit limits.

questions.question: Which situation warrants custom (Apex) sharing logic over stamping?
options: Access derived from an external system's runtime computation that a field cannot represent
questions.explanation: When the access-determining data is computed externally and cannot be stamped, Apex Managed Sharing is required. Simple picklist, one-off, and hierarchy cases are declarative.

questions.question: A complex, data-derived access rule cannot be expressed with sharing rules. What is the appropriate mechanism?
options: A public group with static rules
Apex Managed Sharing inserting Share rows with a custom RowCause
questions.explanation: Apex Managed Sharing grants record access programmatically where declarative rules cannot. Public OWD over-exposes, and groups/record types cannot express dynamic data-derived access.

questions.question: A user must access records owned by two different groups. What is the cleanest sharing-rule design?
options: Two ownership-based rules, one per source group, both granting the user's group access
One criteria rule on Owner = User
questions.explanation: Each ownership-based rule shares one source group's records to the target group; combine multiple rules to aggregate sources. Criteria rules and OWD changes do not express 'owned by specific groups' as cleanly.

questions.question: What is the difference between an authenticated external user and the guest user in Experience Cloud?
options: The guest user is the unauthenticated profile with its own restricted sharing; authenticated external users have a profile/license and relationship-based sharing
questions.explanation: The guest profile represents anonymous visitors with minimal, explicit guest sharing; authenticated external users carry a portal license/profile and access via sharing sets tied to their account.

questions.question: Several users who are not managers must collaborate on a single high-value Account, each with a defined role. Which feature fits best?
options: A public group with a sharing rule
An Account Team on that Account
A permission set with View All
questions.explanation: Account Teams provide per-record, owner-managed collaboration with roles and access levels for exactly this ad-hoc need. Groups/rules and OWD changes are population-wide, and View All over-grants.

questions.question: A new custom object should be readable by everyone but editable only by owners. Which OWD should be set?
questions.explanation: Public Read Only grants universal read with owner-only edit. Private would hide records from non-owners, and Public Read/Write would let everyone edit.

questions.question: After enabling 'Use Account Teams' on Opportunity, an org notices opportunities are visible to more people than expected. What is the cause?
options: Every Opportunity now shares to the Account Team members automatically
questions.explanation: 'Use Account Teams' makes each Opportunity inherit the Account's team members automatically, so broad account teams widen opportunity access - the expected, if surprising, behavior.

questions.question: An architect must ensure access to a child object exactly mirrors access to its parent and cannot diverge. Which relationship is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Master-detail couples child access to the parent via Controlled by Parent. Lookup relationships keep access independent, which is the opposite requirement.

questions.question: An org needs record access based on a value computed from a third-party integration, which the sharing-rule builder cannot express. What is the correct solution?
options: Apex Managed Sharing with a scheduled/triggered reconciliation of Share rows
questions.explanation: Runtime-derived access from external data cannot be a declarative rule; Apex Managed Sharing with reconciliation code is the mechanism. The other options cannot express the dynamic condition.

questions.question: Which is the correct comparison between public groups and teams?
options: Teams are org-wide; groups are per-record
Groups are reusable targets for sharing rules across populations; teams grant per-record, owner-managed access
Teams cannot be enabled on Account
questions.explanation: Public groups are reusable, population-level targets for rules; teams are per-record, owner-configured grants. They solve different scale problems and are not interchangeable.

questions.question: Why is a newly created criteria-based sharing rule not instantly granting access?
options: Criteria-based sharing is evaluated asynchronously and may need recalculation; grants appear after processing
questions.explanation: Criteria rules are evaluated asynchronously for new/changed records and edited conditions; until recalculation/processing completes, grants are stale - the expected behavior, not an error.

questions.question: Which scenario is best handled by Account Teams rather than groups or the hierarchy?
options: The owner of each high-value account decides which specific people help on that account, different people per account
All analysts must see all accounts
questions.explanation: Per-record, owner-selected collaboration is precisely what teams do. Fixed populations (analysts) are groups, reporting lines are the hierarchy.

questions.question: An org shares high-value accounts to a recurring set of 15 analysts across two roles, and this set is reused in three sharing rules. Which structure is best?
options: Reference the 15 users individually in each rule
Create a public group with the analysts, then target that group in the rules
Create a permission set for each rule
questions.explanation: A public group centralizes the recurring set so one membership change updates all referencing rules. Rules cannot target individual user lists cleanly, and queues/perm sets do not solve multi-rule targeting.

questions.question: Why might a criteria-based rule not share records that were just stamped with the matching value?
options: The rule needs recalculation and the stamp/rule evaluation is asynchronous
questions.explanation: Criteria rule evaluation and recalculation are asynchronous; after stamp values change, the rule's grants can be stale until recalc processes - the expected behavior to plan for.

questions.question: After adding a criteria-based sharing rule on Account, some records still don't share as expected. What is the most likely cause?
options: The rule was not recalculated after the underlying criteria data changed, or the records don't meet criteria
questions.explanation: Criteria rules evaluate against current field values and existing sharing rows; if the criteria data changed or the rule wasn't recalculated, the grants are stale. Sharing rules never remove access, and OWD Private doesn't block an added rule.

questions.question: Why does changing the OWD of a detail object in a master-detail relationship have no effect on record access?
options: The detail object is a standard object
Detail-child access is Controlled by Parent, so it inherits the master's sharing
questions.explanation: In master-detail, child access is fully inherited from the parent; the child's OWD setting is ignored (Controlled by Parent), so you configure the parent's sharing instead.

questions.question: An org must share all Accounts where Industry = Finance with the Finance Analysts group at Read/Write, keeping OWD Private. Which rule is correct?
options: A criteria-based sharing rule on Industry = Finance targeting the Finance Analysts group
Setting Account OWD to Public Read/Write
questions.explanation: Criteria-based sharing rules grant records matching a field condition to a target group. Ownership-based is for owner-defined sets, and relaxing OWD affects everyone.

questions.question: Which statement about Case Teams is TRUE?
options: They grant access to a specific Case for the named members with a role and access level
questions.explanation: Case Teams are per-record grants to named members on a specific case. They are not org-wide, need no group, and do not affect the hierarchy.

questions.question: What does the RowCause field on a Share record represent?
options: The reason why the share row was created (e.g. your custom managed-sharing reason)
questions.explanation: RowCause records the origin/reason of the share (Manual, Rule, or a custom reason) so you can identify and manage managed-sharing rows. Access level is a separate field.

questions.question: What is the primary data-protection risk of giving external users a high role in the role hierarchy?
options: They gain hierarchy access to records owned below that role, potentially including unrelated internal data
questions.explanation: A high role grants upward-hierarchy access to records owned below it, which can expose unrelated internal data. Place external roles as low as needed.

questions.question: Sensitive child records must NOT be visible just because a user can read the parent. Which design avoids propagation?
options: A lookup relationship with the child object's OWD kept Private and no related-record sharing
An Account Team on the parent
questions.explanation: Lookups do not propagate access, and keeping the child OWD Private (with no related-record sharing) prevents parent access from leaking to children. Master-detail and related-record sharing would couple them.

questions.question: A dashboard summarizes metrics and must NOT reveal other managers' data to a viewer. What is the correct running-user setting?
questions.explanation: Running as the logged-in user filters the dashboard to the viewer's own data access. Running as an admin or owner exposes that person's broader view to every viewer.

questions.question: A summary report can leak what even when the user cannot open individual records? Choose the best description.
options: Nothing, since they can't see records
Aggregate counts/totals across records the user cannot open individually
questions.explanation: Summary reports and dashboards reveal aggregates (counts, sums) that can expose information about records the viewer can't open one by one - a subtle leak to design against.

questions.question: Why must access to Event Monitoring logs be tightly restricted?
options: Audit logs reveal query patterns and data-access behavior that is itself sensitive exposure
questions.explanation: Event monitoring logs capture who queried what and how - exposing them reveals data-access patterns and potential vulnerabilities, so access must be limited to designated admins/analysts.

questions.question: A Big Object stores two years of historical transaction logs for analysts. How should access be governed?
options: Object-level permissions via profile/permission sets, since Big Objects don't support the full OWD/sharing-rule/role model
OWD to Private plus sharing rules
questions.explanation: Big Objects are optimized for large-scale query and do not support the granular OWD/sharing/role model of standard objects; you govern them with object permissions and design data partitioning. The other options assume standard-object sharing that Big Objects lack.

questions.question: Which mechanism controls which Knowledge articles a user can view?
options: Article visibility (internal/customer) plus data category security plus the View Articles permission
questions.explanation: Knowledge article visibility combines the user's Knowledge permission with internal/customer visibility and data categories. It is not record-owner or OWD driven.

questions.question: A scheduled report or Apex job that runs 'as' a high-privilege user can expose what to its recipients/callers?
options: The high-privilege user's data view - a broader data set than any single viewer would otherwise see
questions.explanation: Any run-as context executes with the executing user's broader access; recipients of a run-as report or callers of run-as code can see data beyond their own access. Control the running context to least privilege.

questions.question: A manager creates a report in a public folder; each rep who runs it should see only their own team's data. What preserves this?
options: Leave the report run-as the logged-in user
Set the report to run as the manager
Grant View All to all reps
Move the report to a private folder only
questions.explanation: Reports default to run-as the viewing user, so each rep's results reflect their own sharing - exactly the desired behavior. Running as the manager or granting View All would expose all data to everyone.

questions.question: A user can open an Account record but cannot see a file attached to it. What is the most likely reason?
options: File access is governed separately from record access - the file isn't shared with that user
The Account is a master record
questions.explanation: File sharing is independent of record sharing; a file attached to a record is only visible to users the file is shared with (via sharing settings, libraries, or record sharing when configured). Record access alone does not grant file access.

questions.question: An External Object surfaces data from a partner's system. Who ultimately enforces record-level access to that data?
options: The external data source's own authentication/authorization, with the internal external-object permissions gating who can query at all
A sharing rule on the external object
questions.explanation: External Objects connect to external data; the external system enforces the record-level rules, while internal profile permissions control who may query the external object at all. Internal sharing rules/OWD cannot secure externally-held data.

questions.question: Why does placing a report in a folder a user can open NOT guarantee they can see the report's records?
options: Report results are filtered by the viewer's own sharing/FLS; folder access only controls who can view/edit the report
questions.explanation: Folder access governs access to the report artifact; the DATA shown is filtered by each viewer's record sharing and field security. The two are independent.

questions.question: Which sharing design is MOST likely to cause sharing-table bloat on large data volumes?
options: A restrictive OWD with a few sharing rules to groups
Deep role hierarchy with every record gaining an ancestor row, plus large per-record teams
One criteria rule to a single group
questions.explanation: Deep hierarchies and broad per-record teams each add a share row per granted ancestor/member, multiplying across records. Restrictive OWD with a few group rules keeps the table lean.

questions.question: Why must recalculation paths be part of security testing?
options: Criteria changes, ownership transfers, and rule edits can leave stale or missing grants that only recalculation testing surfaces
Recalc is automatic and always correct
questions.explanation: Testing recalculation catches stale (or missing) share rows after the conditions rules depend on change. Recalc is not cosmetic or always-correct - it must be exercised and validated.

questions.question: Why does sharing-table bloat degrade query performance even on indexed fields?
options: A bloated sharing table weakens the efficiency of the sharing-model joins/queries and can exceed practical index benefits
questions.explanation: Queries must resolve sharing through the sharing table; when it grows enormously, even indexed lookups slow down and the cost of the sharing join dominates - keeping it lean preserves performance.

questions.question: How should an architect avoid expensive sharing recalculation on a large object?
options: Base criteria rules on stable fields, batch ownership changes, and schedule necessary recalcs
questions.explanation: Designing rules on stable fields and batching changes minimizes recalculation. Frequent recalcs, hourly recalc, or disabling sharing are not sound approaches.

questions.question: Why can't a permission set grant a capability to a user who lacks the supporting license?
options: Object/system permissions in a permission set must be compatible with the user's single assigned license, and feature gating blocks incompatible grants
questions.explanation: Each user has one license; permission-set grants must be compatible with it, and license-gated features cannot be granted without the supporting license - the permission set cannot bypass the user's license.

questions.question: Which scenario is most likely a LICENSE limitation rather than a sharing-configuration error?
options: A feature like Experience Cloud, Shield encryption, or Field Audit Trail being unavailable for the org/users
A criteria rule not sharing a record
A page layout missing a field
questions.explanation: Enterprise-grade features (Experience, Shield, Field Audit Trail) are licensed; their absence for users is typically a license-tier limitation, whereas the other options are config/behavior issues.

questions.question: An org with only internal Salesforce CRM licenses must give partners portal access to their accounts. What is the key licensing implication?
options: Experience/community licenses (e.g. Partner Community) are required for external users and sharing sets; without them portal access is not possible
questions.explanation: External-user portal access is an Experience Cloud (community) feature requiring the corresponding licenses. Without them, sharing sets/portal access cannot be configured; Shield/Platform licenses do not provide it.

questions.question: An object holds 50M records and needs three analyst groups to each see a subset by region. What is the most scalable design?
options: Three criteria-based sharing rules (one per region) to the three groups, with a restrictive OWD
questions.explanation: A restrictive OWD plus three coarse criteria rules produces few, group-level share rows - the leanest scalable design. Teams/manual shares/hierarchy would create per-record rows across 50M records.

questions.question: Why must sharing-set-based access be flagged as a licensing concern before design?
options: Sharing sets are an Experience Cloud feature requiring external-user licenses, so internal-only orgs must buy those licenses to use them
questions.explanation: Sharing sets are an Experience Cloud capability for external users; an internal-only license inventory cannot deliver partner access through them without purchasing Experience licenses - a licensing constraint on the design.

questions.question: Why can sharing recalculation be expensive at scale?
options: It rebuilds/validates many share rows across large volumes and can be slow and lock-heavy
questions.explanation: Recalculation recomputes the sharing table for many records; on LDV this is CPU/IO heavy, slow, and can lock tables - so designs should minimize recalc frequency.

questions.question: How can an architect validate the COMPOSITION of a record's effective sharing?
options: Open the record's Sharing detail to see the share-graph rows and their sources (OWD, hierarchy, rules, teams, Apex)
questions.explanation: The Sharing detail lists the share rows and their RowCause/source, revealing exactly which mechanism grants access - essential to catch unexpected grants. Folders, profiles, and backups do not show this.
